## Summary

The Japanese occupiers paid for what they took with a peso they printed themselves, which Filipinos nicknamed "Mickey Mouse money". Hyperinflation was measured: **60 % in January 1944, prices doubling every 44.9 days** (H&K, who call the currency "Japanese War Notes"). By 1944 a box of matches cost more than 100 of these pesos. At liberation the currency was withdrawn and worth nothing.

## Causes

- **An occupier paying with its own paper.** The notes had no reserve and could not be redeemed;
  the army issued them for supplies and labour.
- **Japan claimed a monopoly on money.** Holding guerrilla currency was outlawed, and offenders
  were arrested or executed (Wikipedia). Two currencies competed anyway.

## Timeline

- **1942** — the occupation peso is issued (1 centavo to 10 pesos).
- **1943–1945** — 100, 500 and 1,000-peso notes are added as prices climb.
- **Jan 1944** — the peak month, 60 % (H&K).
- **Dec 1944** — the episode ends in the H&K table.

## The end

The currency did not end through a reform: it ended with the army that issued it. Savings held in occupation pesos were simply lost.

## Lessons

- An occupation currency is a tax on the occupied, collected through prices.
- People kept a parallel money (pre-war pesos, guerrilla notes) as long as they dared.
